title: Chapter LVI

teacherSummary.text: Lady Catherine arrives unexpectedly and demands that Elizabeth promise never to marry Darcy, claiming he is engaged to Anne. Elizabeth refuses to promise anything, defending her right to choose.

vocabulary.context: You are to understand, Miss Bennet, that I came here with the determined resolution of carrying my purpose; nor will I be dissuaded from it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dissuade”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To start or spring up suddenly
vocabulary.context: The upstart pretensions of a young woman without family, connections, or fortune.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “upstart”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A thing of very little value or importance
vocabulary.context: “Miss Bennet,” replied her ladyship, in an angry tone, “you ought to know that I am not to be trifled with.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “trifle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Furniture or outfit, whether useful or ornamental
vocabulary.context: It was too early in the morning for visitors, and besides, the equipage did not answer to that of any of their neighbours.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “equipage”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A piece of cloth, or other suitable material, sewed or otherwise fixed upon a garment to repair or strengthen it, esp
vocabulary.context: I know it all; that the young man’s marrying her, was a patched-up business, at the expense of your father and uncle.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “patch”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: “It ought to be so; it must be so, while he retains the use of his reason.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “retain”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + tain (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: As they passed through the hall, Lady Catherine opened the doors into the dining-parlour and drawing-room, and pronouncing them, after a short survey, to be decent looking rooms, walked on.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pronouncing”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To treat in a violent manner
vocabulary.context: No principle of either, would be violated by my marriage with Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “violate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “Because honour, decorum, prudence, nay, interest, forbid it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “decorum”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A kind of small umbrella used by women as a protection from the sun
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth obeyed, and running into her own room for her parasol, attended her noble guest downstairs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “parasol”: sol (Latin solus, "alone" / sol, "sun"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Aristocratic marriages were often arranged to keep wealth in families.

significance: Elizabeth's defiance is a high point of independence against rank.
discussionQuestions: What gives Elizabeth the courage to defy Lady Catherine?
Where does conflict appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LVI,” how does Austen show the great confrontation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LVI, how does Austen develop the idea of the great confrontation? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the conflict in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LVI develops the idea of the great confrontation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LVI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its conflict shape the reader's understanding of the great confrontation. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LVI suggests about the great confrontation. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's conflict and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses conflict in Chapter LVI to complicate the reader's understanding of the great confrontation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the great confrontation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LVI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the great confrontation follows or bends those conventions, using the conflict as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LVI and its treatment of the great confrontation. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's conflict and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LVI as evidence for a larger claim about the great confrontation in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the great confrontation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Conflict

As they passed through the hall, Lady Catherine opened the doors into the dining-parlour and drawing-room, and pronouncing them, after a short survey, to be decent looking rooms, walked on.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What gives Elizabeth the courage to defy Lady Catherine? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are dissuaded, upstart, trifled, equipage, patched. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “You are to understand, Miss Bennet, that I came here with the determined resolution of carrying my purpose; nor will I be dissuaded from it.” Webster's says: To advise or exhort against. Now the word history: “dissuade”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “upstart”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “trifle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Aristocratic marriages were often arranged to keep wealth in families. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's defiance is a high point of independence against rank. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for conflict.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see conflict, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the great confrontation.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Conflict, Characterization, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of conflict. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Elizabeth obeyed, and running into her own room for her parasol, attended her noble guest downstairs. As they passed through the hall, Lady Catherine opened the doors into the dining-parlour and drawing-room, and pronouncing them, after a short survey, to be decent looking rooms, walked on.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Conflict, Characterization, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LVI,” how does Austen show the great confrontation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the great confrontation, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how conflict shapes the great confrontation. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
